title: Management of refractory postpneumonectomy empyema with bronchopleural fistula
case_text:
A 39-year-old female had a history of tuberculosis spanning 11 years. Prior to admission to our clinic, the observations included the following:
Ineffective tuberculosis treatment over 2 years (2004-2006)
Combined resection of the right lung in 2006
Tuberculosis relapse in 2012, with failure of conservative treatment
A final right lung pneumonectomy in 2015, complicated by right main bronchial stump insufficiency (BSI) and pleural empyema
Transpleural reamputation of the right main bronchial stump with simultaneous 8-rib thoracoplasty on the 21st day after surgery, again complicated by BSI and pleural empyema
Six unsuccessful attempts at endobronchial valve implantation, one resulting in clinical death
Unsuccessful right thoracostomy 4 months later.
In June 2016, the patient was admitted to our clinic. The patient (height = 165 cm, weight = 50 kg, and body mass index = 18 kg/cm2) presented with shortness of breath on exertion even when talking, severe exhaustion, and deformed chest with thoracic defect up to 4 cm in the right auxiliary region with purulent discharge and air leakage. Removal of tampons located in the pleural empyema cavity led to aphonia. Computed tomography (CT) scan [Figure 1] showed a wide tracheal defect.
Fibrobronchoscopy revealed a dehiscent short stump of the right main bronchus extending from the lateral wall of the trachea (2 cm x 2.5 cm).
Basic spirometry testing revealed vital capacity (VC) - 36.7% and forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) - 30.6%.
Arterial blood gas analysis revealed pO2-72 mm and pCO2-38.7 mmHg.
Microbiological analysis of the fluid from empyema cavity revealed the growth of Pseudomonas aeruginosa by the BASTEC method and Mycobacterium tuberculosis with multiple drug resistance (H, R, Rb, Z, E, Fq, Pt, Pas, and Cs).
There was additionally a history of chronic viral hepatitis C, chronic left otitis media, chronic bronchitis, chronic gastritis, and postoperative plexitis and contracture of the right shoulder joint.
Given all this, a radical intervention to eliminate BSI was postponed for 2 months, during this time the pleural cavity was irrigated via videothoracoscopy.
Following treatment, the patient's condition improved: a 5-kg body weight increase and greater physical activity tolerance - the 6-min walk test (6MWT) demonstrated that she could walk 430 m. No data were available for her performance of 6MWT on admission due to severe exhaustion. Re-examination showed overall improvement in pulmonary function testing (VC - 41.5% and FEV1-36.5%) and arterial blood gas analysis (pO2-78 mmHg and pCO2-31.5 mmHg).
The patient underwent the first operative stage: Transsternal transpericardial wedge-shaped resection of the tracheal bifurcation (duration: 4 h, blood loss: 250 ml). The bifurcation area consisted of empyema with a wide fistula. The parts of the trachea and the left main bronchus were excised wedge-shaped [Figures 2 and 3]. The resulting defect was sutured with separate atraumatic sutures in a transverse manner [Figures 2-4]. Postoperatively, the patient had no further complications.
Thoracomyoplasty was performed 2 months later. The transverse processes of the thoracic vertebrae and posterior segments of 2-5 ribs were resected, the peripheral part of the right main bronchial stump was excised, the postoperative period was uncomplicated and the empyema cavity eliminated.
On the final CT scans [Figure 3], the right hemithorax was deformed after thoracoplasty. No residual cavity was found and no bronchopleural fistula was observed and left-lung volume preserved. Pulmonary parenchyma was without changes, the lung aerating normally.
A follow-up examination 4 years later revealed an 8 kg weight gain [Figure 4], no exacerbations of pulmonary tuberculosis and satisfactory lung function test results with VC - 46.5%, FEV1-34.2% and arterial blood gas analysis pO2-79 mmHg, pCO2-31.2 mmHg.

You are an expert clinician–educator in tropical and infectious diseases.
Your job is to transform a published clinical case report into a standardized admission diagnostic teaching case following the Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology.

In terms of style, model your output on NEJM’s Clinicopathologic Conferences ("Case Records of the Massachusetts General Hospital").

RULES (Read Carefully — No Exceptions):
1. SOURCE FIDELITY:
   - Extract facts ONLY from the supplied case report.
   - Do NOT invent, embellish, or smooth out missing clinical data.
   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Tuberculosis
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: refractory postpneumonectomy empyema with bronchopleural fistula
